title: Idea index
text:
Consolidated from three repos — kath-a-log, spi-m-o, applications. Overarching question (from big-picture.qmd): what is the marginal value of information in emergency epidemic intelligence — is SPI-M fit for purpose? Spine is the evaluation triad of credibility (quality) / relevance (value) / legitimacy (trust), plus two cross-cutting themes (history, workforce).


mindmap
  root((Is SPI-M fit for purpose?))
    Credibility - was the science accurate and honest
      Calibrate the consensus estimates
      Audit the uncertainty language
      Measure model independence
      Packaged as Consensus Audit Framework grant
    Relevance - did it improve decisions
      Value of information data to estimate to decision
      What users actually value
      Does more modelling help
    Legitimacy - who was responsible and to whom
      Responsibility and accountability of advisory numbers
      Two modes of production SPI-M-O vs ONS
      Impact tracing outputs to policy
    Process - how was consensus made
      How consensus is made and could be improved
    History and sociology
      History of SPI-M
      Is SPI-M a role model
    Workforce and capacity
      Map the expertise network and careers
    Synthesis and design output
      Comparative institutional design
      Field-wide evaluation standards







Idea: score how accurate the weekly consensus R / growth-rate estimates were against a retrospective gold standard, and explain the variation.
Rationale: consensus R was central to UK COVID policy; no external calibration published. Inverts McCabe et al 2024 (they asked whether ONS-CIS could recover the consensus; this asks whether the consensus was any good).
Approach: gov R/growth series (May 2020–Dec 2022) vs inc2prev (Abbott & Funk) from ONS-CIS; proper scoring rules (interval score, 90% CI); handle lags/rolling averages; stratify by variant phase, evidence type, contributor count, inter-model agreement. Model accuracy as a function of those drivers (triangulate with interviews). Fuller designs: value-of-information and decision-impact scoring, re-running contemporary models via CrystalCast; test rounding/combination alternatives (assumption-similarity weighting, Bayesian model averaging).
Natural experiment: July 2021 handover of Rt aggregation from SPI-M-O to JBC/UKHSA — accuracy and uncertainty language with group discussion (pre) vs without (post).
Interpretation: hypothesis that a simple average over variable inputs is more biased than a single model on a consistent data stream. Prelim: ~19% of consensus estimates got the trend direction wrong (caveat: ONS-CIS excluded closed settings, so consensus could occasionally beat “truth”).
Folds: former A1, A2, A3, K1.
Source: explore-r-gr.qmd; R/process-r-gr.R; application-scientific.qmd





Idea: test whether the probabilistic language in consensus statements was calibrated to the quantitative evidence and internally consistent.
Approach: code statement PDFs against the PHIA “probability yardstick”, IPCC calibrated-uncertainty language, Spiegelhalter’s ladder, or GRADE; grep tooling exists (R/phia-language.R, R/parse-pdf.R); quanteda/widyr for pairwise statement similarity. Does the narrative (“we are confident Rt is…”) match the number?
Interpretation: empirical audit of language–quantity consistency. Responds to COVID Inquiry para 9.118 (minutes should state confidence level and drivers of uncertainty).
Source: phia-language.R; research-map.mm.md





Idea: open the black box of group deliberation, which shapes policy advice yet is almost undocumented.
Approach: Benchmark SPI-M practice against validated protocols (SHELF/IDEA/DELPHI/SEE) and link deviations to calibration.
Interpretation: best-practice guidelines (? GRADE-like certainty + strength) for producing consensus statements; what AI changes about consensus.

Idea: measure genuine diversity among contributing models — a consensus over redundant models is falsely confident.
Approach: reconstruct each model’s structural assumptions via elicitation; build a per-model DAG for a “genealogy of shared assumptions” (Knutti/Masson); compute a similarity index vs consensus accuracy. Calibrate individual components for “internal model discrepancy” (upper bound on value of model improvement). Adapt the Harvey-Leybourne-Newbold encompassing test on the model submission archive to separate independent from redundant model pairs.
Interpretation: taxonomy of error; diversity of methods vs number of models.
Source: case-for-support.qmd; research-map.mm.md

Packaged: Consensus Audit Framework (UK Metascience grant) bundles Calibrate the consensus estimates, Audit the uncertainty language, and Measure model independence into WP1 corpus calibration + WP2 interviews + WP3 a reusable audit framework transferable to IPCC/WHO/food-safety bodies. Source: application-ukms-spim.qmd








Idea: trace value along the whole chain — how much each surveillance stream reduced Rt uncertainty, and the mortality cost of decision errors.
Approach: (data) collate every surveillance source cited in COVID consensus statements (cases, hospitalisations, deaths; ONS-CIS, REACT, CoMix); estimate posterior-uncertainty reduction per stream. (decision) systematic review of SPI-M statements 2009–2022 for implied Rt/excess-mortality decision thresholds; trace SPI-M → SAGE → government decisions via Inquiry records; map Rt to excess mortality via age/sex/region IFR.
Interpretation: surveillance-priority guide for future outbreaks; whether over- or under-reliance carried measurable health costs. This is the master “marginal value of information” framing (VOI on two axes: epidemiological vs public-health information), with SPI-M as flagship case study.
Source: case-for-support.qmd; big-picture.qmd; planning-big-picture.md





Idea: elicit what makes a “good” forecast for the people using it.
Approach: discrete choice experiment across model characteristics (performance, interpretability, context specificity, known past performance), modeller characteristics (team trust, in-house vs external, modifiability), outbreak characteristics — how much better must a single model be to beat the ensemble? Complement with the “working alliance” (goal/task/bond) model to test whether advice actually changes decision-maker practice.
Interpretation: reveals attributes of the problem that drive decisions
Source: users.qmd; research-context.qmd





Idea: field-wide review of whether aggregating many models into ensembles improved decision-making.
Rationale: process factors (onboarding, consensus time, resources) and impact factors (relevance, communication, acceptance) are rarely reported; infrastructure was scaled with almost no evaluation of decision support.
Approach: European COVID Hub case study; drivers of component performance; decade-long systematic review of multi-model collaborations.
Interpretation: predictive accuracy is not usefulness; weighs benefits against the costs of collaborative advisory work.
Source: EMS-Lugano-abstract-DRAFT.md









Idea: whether and how SPI-M-O should be held to account for the numbers it produced.
Approach: treat Medley’s three claimed “invaluable” functions (peer review, uncertainty emphasis, shared responsibility) as evaluable claims with risks as well as benefits; map onto OSR “Quality, Value, Trust”, the Aqua Book, and the Orange Book “three lines of defence”; analyse how SPI-M’s function shifted across those lines and what QA fits each; review OSR casework (4 COVID R requests 2020-21, all “informal discussion”), UKHSA’s 2022 voluntary compliance, and government QA codes (Macpherson, BEIS, NAO, Scientific Advisory Committees code); JCVI as routine advice lacking QA.
Interpretation: suspicion SPI-M is nominally Line 3 (independent review) but operated as Line 2, at times Line 1 (guiding policy via headline R); diffusion-of-responsibility moral hazard. Central question: how far should advisory bodies be held to the same account as official statistics? Explicit role definition would have reduced both over- and under-reliance.
Source: evaluation.qmd; regulation.qmd; research-map.mm.md





Idea: compare a demand-driven, voluntary, ad hoc expert group (SPI-M-O) against a supply-driven, funded, routine producer (ONS excess deaths).
Rationale: both produce unobservable, lagged, censored, policy-salient estimands; the difference is mode of production.
Approach: compare on Quality (real-time evaluation, peer review), Value (uncertainty, risk expression), Trust (responsibility allocation); documentary analysis + OSR compliance review.
Interpretation: comparative case study + institutional design recommendations.
Source: rt-excess-deaths.qmd





Idea: link SPI-M’s probabilistic outputs to documented policy influence.
Approach: database of probabilistic statements cross-referenced against the Inquiry witness-statement corpus; trace membership’s work via ORCID; policy use via Hansard, FOI, Overton.
Interpretation: empirical map of advice-to-policy uptake.
Source: consensus-statements.qmd; sources.qmd









Idea: a fair narrative account of how and why SPI-M worked, across successive outbreaks, for a readership wider than modellers — and why it has gone unevaluated.
Approach: by outbreak / by outbreak phase (detection, wave, stand-down), against credibility/relevance/legitimacy criteria. Chronology 2001 FMD → 2009 H1N1 → 2014 Ebola → 2016 Zika → 2018 Cygnus → 2020-22 COVID → 2025 Pegasus. Methods: cohort surveys across outbreaks; key-informant + random one-off-participant interviews; text mining of witness statements (term frequency, topic modelling, sentiment, co-mention networks); FOI. Precedent detail: H1N1 2009 evaluation question set; Exercise Pegasus 2025 after-action review of LSHTM/CMMID participation.
Interpretation: load-bearing threads — Hine Review (2012) urged clearer evidence/advice demarcation and SPI-B integration; recurring tension between SPI-M as synthesiser vs challenger of UKHSA; Pegasus shifted back to champion/challenge, confusing SPI-M’s function; the “missing middle” argument that the Inquiry inhibited scientific evaluation (burnout, turnover, no incentives, survivor bias). Tests survivor bias and a Matthew effect of path dependency.
Source: natural-history.qmd; history.qmd; inquiry-evaluation.qmd; 2009-spimo.qmd; LSHTM Pegasus response.qmd





Idea: interrogate why SPI-M is treated as best practice and whether that is warranted or transferable.
Approach: multiple role models for different domains of model value; “knights of the round table vs champion/challenger” for managing many models; conceptual thesis that each field has a canonical baseline model (SIR, energy balance, supply/demand) against which development is implicitly judged.
Interpretation: for what and for whom does SPI-M “work”, and are its lessons context-specific or exportable?
Source: role-models.qmd; research-map.mm.md









Idea: map the shape and sustainability of UK outbreak-modelling expertise.
Rationale: a core critique of the advisory infrastructure was groupthink; recruitment relies on personal relationships and a narrow pool.
Approach: COVID-anchored citation network (UK-affiliated authors), cluster by domain/method, verify via survey, compare vs national risk register; survival analysis of responder careers (cohort by outbreak; outcomes = institution change / mental-health diagnosis / exit).
Interpretation: test the Matthew effect (early responders gaining centrality); blind spots vs national priorities; whether recruitment should counteract seniority bias; possible living map of expertise with the SPI-M chair / JUNIPER.
Source: uk-modelling-expertise.qmd; instutitional-sop.qmd; All applications.md









Idea: turn the evaluation into design guidance by comparing alternative institutional structures.
Approach: compare WHO / UKHSA / SPI-M via survey, interview, focus group, and a discrete choice experiment presenting alternative structures and conflicts; treat “one advisor vs many” and “champion/challenger vs consensus” as explicit design axes.
Interpretation: which institutional design decision-makers prefer; guidelines for a more structured, ethical, balanced advisory process.
Source: All applications.md; wellcome-first-draft.md





Idea: a PRISMA-equivalent minimum reporting standard for epidemic forecast evaluation; a JUNIPER network theme on modelling evaluation using the credibility/relevance/legitimacy triad.
Approach: formal Delphi to set the standard.
Interpretation: field-level infrastructure so future advisory work is reportable and evaluable by default.
Source: research-map.mm.md; evaluation.qmd (kath-a-log); juniper.md







NIHR Postdoctoral Award (“Recalibrating consensus-based science”): Calibrate the consensus estimates, Measure model independence, Value of information: data → estimate → decision, Responsibility and accountability of advisory numbers, Map expertise network and career trajectories. case-for-support.qmd
UK Metascience (SPI-M) — Consensus Audit Framework: Calibrate the consensus estimates, Audit the uncertainty language, Measure model independence. application-ukms-spim.qmd
UK Metascience (HPAI) — AI vs human consensus: How consensus is made and could be improved. application-ukms-hpai.qmd
Wellcome ECR — marginal value of modelling: Value of information: data → estimate → decision, What users actually value, How consensus is made and could be improved, History of SPI-M. case-for-support.qmd
LSHTM GAP — fit-for-purpose modelling: Value of information: data → estimate → decision, Does more modelling help?, History of SPI-M. gap.md
JUNIPER Fellowship — network theme on evaluation: Field-wide evaluation standards. juniper.md

Binary decks not opened: kath-a-log PDFs “2026-03-24 Evaluation & responsible modelling.pdf”, “2026-03-19 Sherratt HPRU-Pegasus.pdf”.

title: COVID-19 R and growth rate estimates in England
text: R and growth rate are fundamental summaries of how an epidemic is spreading1. During COVID-19, R in particular was used directly to inform national and subnational political action. In the UK, national government published R and growth rate estimates for the UK, nations, and subnational regions. Esimates were published weekly from May 2020, to December 2022.

title: COVID-19 R and growth rate estimates in England
text:
How accurate was the consensus?
We don’t typically collect data on R directly, as it is an average of transmission chains. This makes it difficult to evaluate how accurate any estimate truly is.
However, retrospectively, we can compare these real-time estimates against a “best” (ex post) estimate of the same quantity. This uses prevalence estimated by the ONS Community Infection Survey to calculate underlying ongoing transmission. This is the “gold standard” because the CIS was designed to represent the full population in a random sample (in a pre-established protocol designed specifically to collect this kind of data). R/growth rate were estimated with the inc2prev model (Abbott & Funk 2021)5.






NotePrevious work





Descriptively, Medley 2022 reports the consensus process of SPI-M-O. Both Maishman et al 2022 and Park et al 2023 report methods for combining R and growth rate estimates after it was taken on by DSTL/JBC/UKHSA.
Work by McCabe et al 2024 models the calibration of modelled estimates from ONS-CIS data, to the published consensus model estimates.









TipWhen might the consensus model be ‘better’ than the gold standard estimate?





The ONS-CIS survey didn’t sample in closed care settings: care homes, hospitals. However, these settings have their own particular transmission patterns. This is important because the national R is intended to summarise across all transmission patterns. So when these closed settings had very high levels of transmission, their specific (and unusual) pattern could be driving national level epidemic dynamics. The ONS-CIS study would miss this effect.
So, if one or more of the modellers contributing to the consensus can calibrate their estimate to reflect these different settings, then the consensus model might well be a better single summary statistic.









NoteComparison with McCabe et al 2024





McCabe et al assess the potential of the ONS-CIS study to recover the consensus estimate. This is the opposite approach to that I’ve taken above. The authors model R and growth rate from the ONS-CIS data using a smooth spline. They then use the consensus estimates as a predictor for their ONS-CIS based R value. They also add a lag/lead time of ±20 days on the timeseries of consensus estimates; and keep only the consensus timeseries for “the time lag and knot value under which R^2 is maximised”.
They evaluate against three metrics: R^2 from linear regression; Spearman rank correlation; and “agreement proportion”, whether the consensus/comparator point estimate agreed on the direction of growth (i.e. estimate against threshold of 1 for R, 0 for growth rate). Overall results are reported as:

Depending on nation and parameter, up to 77% of the variance in the government-published estimates can be explained by the ONS-based estimates, providing evidence of the suitability of this singular data stream to track the epidemic

For example, for England, they use an -8 day lagged timeseries of the consensus estimate to predict their ONS-CIS based R value. They report a “maximum” R^2 of 0.71, Spearman correlation 0.85, agreement proportion 0.81.
In contrast, my motivation is the reverse: was the consensus estimate any good, relative to a best estimate of R/growth rate.
As an alternative framing… consider McCabe et al’s agreement proportion for England (0.81). This might suggest that even in the best possible scenario for the consensus model (fit to as much of the comparator model as possible, with any amount of time lag or spline knots) - still, 19% of the consensus estimates didn’t even represent the correct direction of the epidemic trend (growth/decline).
My hypothesis is that the consensus is much more prone to bias and error given the method of taking a simple average across very variable inputs. By comparison, a single model using a consistent single data stream should be less biased.




Ex post comparison


Code
i2p <- read_csv("https://github.com/epiforecasts/inc2prev/raw/refs/heads/main/outputs/estimates_national.csv") 

i2p <- i2p |>
filter(variable == "England") |>
select(date, region = variable, value_type = name, value_lower = q10, value_upper = q90) |>
filter(value_type %in% c("R", "r")) |>
mutate(value_lower = ifelse(value_lower == "r", value_lower*100, value_lower),
value_upper = ifelse(value_upper == "r", value_upper*100, value_upper),
value_type = ifelse(value_type == "r", "growth rate", "R"),
model = "inc2prev")


Let’s compare.
The inc2prev estimate is calculated daily, to 4 d.p. Naively plotting this directly against the consensus model estimates:


Code
r_gr2 <- r_gr |>
rename(value_lower_consensus = value_lower,
value_upper_consensus = value_upper)

comp <- left_join(i2p, r_gr2, by = c("date", "region", "value_type"))

plot_estimates_comp <- function(region, data, value_type = "R") {
    data |>
filter(region == {{region}}) |>
filter(value_type %in% {{value_type}}) |>
mutate(reference = ifelse(value_type == "R", 1, 0)) |>
ggplot(aes(x = date)) +
geom_linerange(aes(ymin = value_lower_consensus, ymax = value_upper_consensus), alpha = 0.4, lwd=0.3, col = "#af8dc3") +
geom_point(aes(y=value_upper_consensus), size = 0.3, col = "#af8dc3") +
geom_point(aes(y=value_lower_consensus), size = 0.3, col = "#af8dc3") +
geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = value_lower, ymax = value_upper), alpha = 0.2, col = "grey50", fill = "grey50") +
geom_line(aes(y = reference), lty=1, col="grey50") +
geom_vline(aes(xintercept = as.Date("2021-07-21")), lty=2, col="grey50") +
facet_wrap(~value_type, ncol=1, scales = "free_y") +
labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimate (90% CI)", caption = "SPI-M-O consensus (bars) and retrospective estimate from infection survey (inc2prev)",
title = paste({{region}}, "COVID-19 epidemic indicators")) +
theme(legend.position = "bottom")
}
plot_estimates_comp("England", data = comp, value_type = "R")









To make it a fairer comparison with the weekly consensus statements, we can round inc2prev estimates to 1 d.p. and keep only the days that overlap with the consensus.
Plotting this comparison directly against the consensus range:


Code
comp_trunc <- comp |>
mutate(
    #across(c(value_lower, value_upper), ~ zoo::rollmean(.x, k=7)),
    across(c(value_lower, value_upper), ~ round(.x, digits = 1))) |>
    filter(date %in% r_gr$date)

plot_estimates_comp("England", data = comp_trunc, value_type = "R")

title: COVID-19 R and growth rate estimates in England
text:
Further work

Next steps
The next thing to do will be to assess calibration using proper scoring rules.
To do this we will need to

decide on one or more metrics, and score

consider whether to assess only the 90% CI, or the implied point estimate
think about lags between the two sources (maybe a 7-day rolling average on inc2prev to reflect the 7-day cadence of SPI-M?)
consider appropriate stratification/summarisation

explore language of the narrative consensus statements to assess

internal consistency: are narrative claims like “we are confident that Rt is…” consistent with the quantitative estimate each week?
external calibration: do such claims


use the formal language of uncertainty at all, and


how well calibrated are they, if so?






Some other ideas

Parametric uncertainty
How does accuracy of the consensus change over time, what predicts and explains this, and which of those factors can be changed?
Approach: model the error as a combination of factors -

Data: Availability of each data stream; reliability of each data stream (data revisions)
Epidemiology: trend, variants, restrictions

plus

Number of models
Sources of individual models
Quality of group discussion

plus

Decision critical time-points
Responsible owner for the consensus estimate

… and triangulate with qualitative interviews, to assess model credibility at each stage of model evaluation.


Structural uncertainty
What are the risks/rewards of the facilitated group, vs independent contributions? After 2021, Rt estimates were sent directly to JBC for aggregation, and formed much less of the SPI-M-O group discussion. This could suggest a ‘natural experiment’ design to look at accuracy with/without responsibility for aggregation.
Could look at:

individual models vs consensus vs ex post
alternative combinations vs equal weighting
narrative expression of uncertainty created with discussion (pre-JBC) and without discussion (post-JBC)




Some more ideas
Three more involved suggestions for evaluation:
Observational

Comparison


Similar to McCabe et al 2024:

using inc2prev for the comparator
Using the interval score for the 90% CI range, instead of the R^2, to get at both sharpness/calibration
Estimates of value of information and translating to decision impact (i.e. effect of lockdown timing on health)

Comparison with contemporary estimates contributing to the ensemble presented above (e.g. rerunning code or via CrystalCast)


Combination


Estimates were reported to 1 d.p; were estimates from each group rounded before or after combination? (Even such a small method point creates an impact…)
What was the effect of consensus discussion; did calibration differ pre/post the handover to JBC6?
Alternative combinations based on harmony of assumptions of e.g. generation time

include only those with similar assumptions (within some range)
use all, but weight by similarity
use all, but weight by retrospective calibration: suggesting what could happen if we had some idea of the best model, but weren’t sure; I think this might get at something like Bayesian model averaging



Elicitating evaluation


Judgements of quality

Participants

those who produced the estimates
those who used them
public aware of them

Show time-series of consensus estimates with light explanation
Ask for confidence in estimate by e.g.

overall judgement of quality, trust
calibration of weekly point / 90% CI (eg interactive)

Multifactorial conditions: show one or more data streams from

estimated infection incidence
accurate case, death data
real-time case, death data

Compare against ‘observed’ accuracy as above

title: COVID-19 R and growth rate estimates in England
text:
Appendix






NoteReading

NoteNotes from source data





Copied from the published data tables
Estimates for R and growth rates are shown as a range, and the true values are likely to lie within this range. Tables 1 and 2 provide a time series of contemporary estimates, which were calculated using the data available at the time and do not necessarily represent the current understanding of R and growth rates for those dates. Estimates have not been revised to include new data.
From 2 April 2021, UK estimates for the R value and growth rate are no longer produced. Given the increasingly localised approach to managing the epidemic, particularly between nations, UK level estimates are less meaningful than previously, and are more easily biased by the models combined in their calculation. SPI-M considers estimates of the R value and growth rates for the four nations and NHS England regions to be more robust and useful metrics than those for the whole UK.
As of 26 March 2021, the approach to combining the R values and growth rate has been normalised, so that modelling groups now submit a time series of estimates and a given date across all models is used, rather than their most recent estimates. This makes the estimation more consistent and robust, with little to no difference to the range.
When the numbers of cases or deaths are at low levels and/or there is a high degree of variability in transmission across a region, then care should be taken when interpreting estimates of R and the growth rate. For example, a significant amount of variability across a region due to a local outbreak may mean that a single average value does not accurately reflect the way infections are changing throughout that region.
R and growth rates are not the only important measures of the epidemic, and should be considered alongside other measures of the spread of disease. In particular, the number of new cases of the disease identified during a specified time period (incidence), and the proportion of the population with the disease at a given point in time (prevalence). If R equals 1 with 100,000 people currently infected, it is a very different situation to R equals 1 with 1,000 people currently infected.
As of 30 April 2021, the reliability indicator for estimates has changed. Prior to this date, daily deaths in a region averaged over a 10-day period were used when calculating an estimate’s reliability score, to determine whether it was based on very few cases in a particular area. These data were agreed to be the most reliable data stream when the indicator was developed in summer 2020. Over recent months, the number of deaths has been driven down to very low levels due to lockdown and the impact of the COVID-19 vaccination programme, consequently reducing reliability scores for many regions. As a result, the number of individuals admitted to hospital with COVID-19 and inpatients newly diagnosed with COVID-19 have replaced deaths as an indicator for whether the estimate is based on very few cases in a region.

Data table notes

Estimates for R and growth rates are shown as a range, and the true values are likely to lie within this range.

Please see point 7 in Notes_and_defintions.

If R equals 1 with 100,000 people currently infected, it is a very different situation to R equals 1 with 1,000 people currently infected.
On 22 October, the regional estimates of R and growth rate were paused until we gain a full understanding of the impact of the reported incident of false negative results on estimates in the South West, South East and London
On 27 October regional estimates of R and growth rate resumed for all regions except the South West. This is following confidence that the impact of the incorrect negatives is unlikely to materially impact the estimates for regions outside of the South West. Estimates for the South West will remain paused until we gain a full understanding of the impact of the reported incident (the incorrect negative PCR test results) on estimates in this region. However, the UKHSA is confident that R is above 1 in the South West and that the epidemic is growing in this region.
On 5 November, the regional estimate of R and growth rate resumed for the South West. This is following confidence that the incorrect PCR test results are unlikely to have materially impacted on the estimates for this region.

title: SPI-M-O research notebook
text: Notebook looking at the UK government’s COVID-19 scientific advisory process, specifically SPI-M-O (Scientific Pandemic Influenza group on Modelling, Operational subgroup).

title: SPI-M-O research notebook
text:
Context
General overview / current thinking presented in April 2026

title: Evaluating SPI-M-O
text:
Graham Medley summarises SPI-M-O’s consensus process as performing three “invaluable” functions:
While Medley’s view is strictly positive, I think each of these also hold risks as well as benefits. I also think these could in fact be evaluated, at least to some degree. These functions also prompts some quite specific questions for the design of new advisory structures.
As a side note, and a rationale for using these three functions rather than some other: I think this three-part structure maps nicely to the “Quality”, “Value”, and “Trust” framework used for evaluating official statistics (see: Office for Statistics Regulation). (I’m aware SPI-M-O certainly does not produce official statistics. But I don’t think that should stop us from holding the work up to the same level of scrutiny just to see what falls out.)
Here are some notes and sketches on how evaluation could proceed, based on the “after action review” format.

title: Evaluating SPI-M-O
text:
peer review

What was supposed to happen?
SPI-M-O as a group is motivated by the idea that comparison from multiple sources of expertise both provides quality assurance and improves overall quality. This has changed form over multiple national crises that have leaned on modelling work. For example, during H1N1 SPI-M-O participants were tasked with critiquing a single model owned by the Health Protection Agency, rather than providing primary modelling work (see: history).
This process also echoes structured elicitation methods, that are designed to provide multiple comparison while mitigating the biases that group dynamics are prone to (e.g. anchoring, halo effects). (Notably, the UK government already uses SEE protocols in the Government Office for Science Foresight team (the “Futures playbook”).)
Given the intended assurance and improvement of quality, policy audiences might reasonably expect that SPI-M-O work at least matches the quality standard expected of central government analysis (the “Aqua Book”).


What actually happened?
In practice, peer review meant independent teams each contributing estimates through their own methods, then comparing them in group discussion. Fairly little of this has been formally evaluated as far as I know. Funk (2021) evaluated short-term forecasts in 2020. Some groups have published retrospective evaluations of their own work (Keeling 2023).
Group outputs focused on the consensus statements. These are accessible in the government archives for Covid-19 and for 2009 H1N1 (see Sources). From individual modelling contributors: where participants submitted background papers, these are published alongside the consensus statements. Individual modelling outputs are otherwise not readily accessible, but should in theory exist (so could be requested) where they were submitted to the Secretariat (weekly Rt estimates, short and medium term incidence projections).
In terms of the process: we have only patchily documented the recruitment, contribution, facilitation, and process for synthesis of the group. There are some various retrospectives published by the participants involved. Otherwise the major source of evidence for this is the COVID-19 Inquiry, and previously the H1N1 Inquiry.


What should happen?

What is the explicit function of SPI-M-O collaboration and/or review? Is the group reviewing each other’s work equally (peers), or reviewing a target analysis (champion/challenger)? How is work compared?
Could/should formal expert elicitation protocols (which generally cover recruitment, facilitation, and synthesis) be adapted to the SPI-M-O context?

title: Evaluating SPI-M-O
text:
emphasis of uncertainty

What was supposed to happen?


What actually happened?
SPI-M-O synthesised expert estimates into a single consensus statement produced by a non-academic secretariat. It reported only the range of Rt (a 90% CI of the mean of all contributing estimates), never a point estimate, which was a deliberate choice to convey uncertainty.

Comparison with retrospective best estimates. For example: even under the most favourable comparison, around 19% of consensus estimates did not correctly identify the direction of Rt (growth versus decline), relative to retrospective best-estimates using EpiEstim (McCabe 2024).



What should happen?

what are the most policy-relevant uncertainties, and how suited is the consensus process for addressing them?
how are estimates of likelihood versus estimates of impact (the two dimensions of risk) handled?
where does the group sit among the three lines of risk management, and is that position agreed, or assumed implictly?

title: Evaluating SPI-M-O
text:
shared responsibility

What was supposed to happen?
Let’s consider the UK Government framework for allocating responsibility for risk management (the Orange Book). This is applied across the whole of government activity:

Operational risk management (i.e. government department)
Internal review and oversight (internal audit)
Independent review



What actually happened?
First, I would be curious to hear where SPI-M-O participants, intepreters, users, and the public would place SPI-M-O on the three lines. My own suspicion is that SPI-M is nominally Line 3 (independent review); when operationalised as SPI-M-O, in practice aligns closer to Line 2; and at times moved toward Line 1, by directly guiding policy (rhetorically, and in some cases actually) via the headline R estimates.
Second, are the SPI-M consensus statements perceived as reporting on risk (overall, or specifically epidemiological risk)? If so, we could assess the statement text against standards for risk reporting, i.e. the Orange Book: Good Practice Guide for Risk Reporting.


What should happen?

how should infrastructure and accountability change when SPI-M takes on the “SPI-M-O” operational role, rather than advisory?
Group advisory settings carry moral hazards, specifically the ‘diffusion of responsibility’ where no single actor is clearly accountable for the group output - how could this be protected against?
what institutional support exists for members during and after operationalisation?

The government has also previously published guidance on ethical research in emergencies. It would be useful to reflect on how these apply to SPI-M-O. Specifically:

Responsibilities that arise for policy-makers include support for emergency preparedness encompassing…

sustainable support for, and enablement of, the infrastructure required to conduct that research, including multi-institution research platforms, priority-setting mechanisms, community engagement plans, and data sharing arrangements
a minimum commitment to ensuring that evidence is generated during or after policy implementation, and that well-designed studies begin as soon as possible after the start of the emergency, addressing evidence gaps that have been prioritised in a transparent and accountable manner
transparency with respect to how emerging evidence has been incorporated into decisions (including decisions not to act), and what underlying values have steered policy and operational choices

title: Potted history
text:
SPI-M-O is called in response to national emergencies, at which point it becomes a formal subcommittee of SAGE. Its mandate is to have two co-chairs (one academic, one policy) and voluntary contribution from academics recruited and invited by those chairs.
This structure grew out of the ad hoc modelling support provided during the 2001 foot and mouth disease outbreak, when groups from Imperial, Cambridge, and Edinburgh were informally asked to assist. Those same groups, and others, were then formally convened under SAGE for the 2009 H1N1 pandemic. The public inquiry that followed (the Hine Review, 2012) recommended that modelling should more clearly demarcate evidence from advice, and better integrate with SPI-B.
After 2009, SPI-M became a standing group attached to the Department of Health, maintaining a network of modellers and keeping preparedness models under review. It was operationalised again for 2014 Ebola, 2016 Zika, and the 2018 simulation Exercise Cygnus, before the sustained activation of 2020-2022.






NotePotted history of SPI-M-O





—UNEDITED: checked for sense but not sources—
2001: Foot and mouth disease
The 2001 FMD outbreak was one of the first times mathematical models were used in real time to directly inform disease control policy in the UK. Three independent modelling groups (Imperial, Cambridge, Edinburgh) produced competing models that informed the controversial contiguous culling policy. The experience was formative but contentious: a retrospective assessment found significant disagreements between them. There was no formal advisory structure equivalent to SPI-M at this point – modellers were brought in ad hoc. The key lesson was that multiple models giving different answers required some mechanism for synthesis and arbitration.
2009: H1N1 (swine flu)
SPI-M-O was formally convened in 2009 for the H1N1 pandemic, as part of the SAGE advisory architecture. This appears to be the first time SPI-M operated as a named, structured body (Medley, 2022). It sat under SAGE alongside SPI-B (behaviour) and SPI-B&C (behaviour and communication). The independent review of the UK’s swine flu response (the Hine Review) examined the advisory structures, and notably recommended modelling should more clearly demarcate evidence from advice and better integrate with SPI-B. Between pandemics, SPI-M became a standing group attached to the Department of Health, maintaining a network of modellers and keeping preparedness models under review. It published a modelling summary for pandemic influenza in 2018 that codified planning assumptions (95% of cases over 9 weeks, 50% in a 3-week peak) used in subsequent exercises.
2014: Ebola
SAGE was activated for the West African Ebola outbreak, and SPI-M-O was convened alongside it. However, COBR convened in July 2014 but SAGE was not activated until October – a three-month gap examined by a Science and Technology Committee report on science in emergencies. Ebola also raised the question of SPI-M’s scope: it was designed around pandemic influenza but was being asked to advise on a very different pathogen and epidemiological context.
2016: Zika
A “Precautionary SAGE” (Pre-SAGE) was activated for Zika, a lighter-touch mechanism for assessing emerging threats when COBR had not been formally convened. SAGE minutes from the Zika response are published.
2016-2018: Exercise Cygnus
Exercise Cygnus (2016) was a Tier 1 national pandemic preparedness exercise simulating an influenza pandemic. SPI-M modelling informed the scenario parameters (absenteeism levels of 30-35% based on SPI-M figures). A notable finding was a “lack of clarity about where modelling data could be accessed from for planning purposes” – local resilience forums didn’t know how to get modelling support. The 2018 SPI-M modelling summary was published after these exercises.
2020-2022: COVID-19
SPI-M-O was activated as a formal sub-group of SAGE at the start of the pandemic – its largest and most sustained activation. As Medley (2022) describes, SPI-M-O operated as a committee of independent academics working with a government secretariat, producing weekly consensus statements addressing questions from policymakers, “largely written by civil servants” but drawing on modelling contributions from members. The R value and growth rate estimates became the group’s signature product. Key developments during COVID included rapid expansion of membership; consensus statements produced at a pace and volume far beyond anything in previous activations; the “equal consensus” model where multiple independent analyses were combined; and growing tension between SPI-M’s role as evidence synthesiser and as challenger of UKHSA’s own analytical capacity.
2025: Exercise Pegasus
Exercise Pegasus was a Tier 1 pandemic preparedness exercise led by DHSC with UKHSA, running September-November 2025. Pegasus shifted back toward a “champion/challenge” model where UKHSA produces primary estimates and the consensus process acts implicitly as peer review. This created confusion about SPI-M’s function: producer of analysis, describer of planned analysis, or peer reviewer of UKHSA analysis. The updated SPI-M terms of reference (January 2025) designate an executive chair from DHSC and a separate academic chair, formalising the dual accountability structure.

Exercise Pegasus was a Tier 1 pandemic preparedness exercise led by DHSC with UKHSA, running September-November 2025. Pegasus shifted back toward a “champion/challenge” model where UKHSA produces primary estimates and the consensus process acts implicitly as peer review. This created confusion about SPI-M’s function: producer of analysis, describer of planned analysis, or peer reviewer of UKHSA analysis. The updated SPI-M terms of reference (January 2025) designate an executive chair from DHSC and a separate academic chair, formalising the dual accountability structure.

title: Comment on the end of the COVID-19 Inquiry
text:
I think the Inquiry actively inhibited scientific evaluation of the work we produced during COVID-19.
I’m coming purely from an academic modeller’s perspective, having spent the last few years gently asking around about who might be interested in evaluating the work of SPI-M. The response has mostly been “we have to wait for the Inquiry”.
I think there are a few reasons contributing to this, and frustratingly I still don’t see a natural avenue for this work. TLDR; I think burn-out, and academic (dis)incentives, have created a “missing middle” in the academic hierarchy where we might otherwise expect this work to come from.
As far as I can tell, up until now we’ve had:

a catastrophic, wildfire level of burn-out among those contributing to the COVID response. We’ve discussed in some depth elsewhere (see: Wellcome Open Research paper)
relatedly, rapid turnover among those who worked on the response - encouraged by the prevalence of short-term contracts in academia
no professional incentives for retrospective evaluation work (i.e. difficult to get quick tractable publications out of evaluation, again a particular issue for those on more junior/short-term contracts)
the Inquiry providing an active disincentive, by (a) quickly and thoroughly using up any of the very limited capacity that we had to reflect on COVID work; (b) providing a diversion for any attempt at reflection, towards a bureaucratic/legalistic/public office framing

I think this has meant we have had neither emotional nor professional capacity for serious, systematic evaluation of COVID-19 work. And that makes it wildly frustrating that the Inquiry did not use whatever capacity we had, well.
Now the Inquiry is over I am still struggling to see where any scientific evaluation can come from, because of the biased losses to institutional memory:

Among those in academia who worked on the real-time COVID response - we still have no capacity for retrospective evaluation, because we’ve spent the last 3-6 years seeking funding for entirely new work. (At best, this newly funded work might include some element of COVID-19 evaluation for background/learning from.) We also represent ‘survivor bias’: I think we’ve seen clear differential attrition among academic careers of responders
Those in academia who might have capacity, tend to be junior researchers - who are unlikely to have directly worked on the response. This would make it very difficult to build a strategy for evaluating across the pandemic work as a whole, not to mention intimidating from the perspective of critiquing the work of one’s (new) colleagues in a small field
